question: The Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) Code is built around four themes. Which of the following is one of those four themes?
options: Prioritise people
Maximise efficiency
Follow orders
Reduce costs
rationale: The NMC Code (2018) is structured around four themes: Prioritise people, Practise effectively, Preserve safety, and Promote professionalism and trust.
source: NMC - The Code

scenario: A medication error reaches a patient and causes moderate harm. The nurse involved is unsure whether to tell the patient.
question: Under the professional duty of candour, what must the nurse do?
options: Wait to see if the patient notices before saying anything
Be open and honest with the patient, tell them when something has gone wrong and apologise
Only report it internally and not tell the patient
Refer the decision entirely to the ward manager and take no personal action
rationale: The professional duty of candour requires healthcare professionals to be open and honest with patients when something goes wrong, to tell them, apologise, and offer support - this is separate from and additional to internal incident reporting.
source: NMC / GMC - professional duty of candour

question: How often must a nurse complete Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) revalidation to remain on the register?
options: Every year
Every two years
Every three years
Every five years
rationale: NMC revalidation is completed every three years, at the point of renewing registration.
source: NMC - revalidation

question: For standard Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) revalidation, how many practice hours and continuing professional development (CPD) hours are required over the three-year period?
options: 300 practice hours and 20 CPD hours
450 practice hours and 35 CPD hours (at least 20 participatory)
600 practice hours and 40 CPD hours
900 practice hours and 50 CPD hours
rationale: Revalidation requires at least 450 hours of registered practice and 35 hours of CPD over three years, of which at least 20 hours must be participatory learning. (900 practice hours applies only to dual registrants.)
source: NMC - revalidation requirements

question: The statutory duty of candour (Care Quality Commission Regulation 20) is triggered by a notifiable safety incident. A notifiable safety incident must, in the reasonable opinion of a healthcare professional, have resulted in (or risk) which minimum level of harm?
options: Any harm, however minor
Low harm
Moderate harm
Only death
rationale: A notifiable safety incident is one that was unintended/unexpected, occurred during a regulated activity, and in a healthcare professional's reasonable opinion has resulted in (or could result in) death, or severe or moderate harm. Moderate harm is the minimum threshold.
source: CQC - Regulation 20 Duty of candour

scenario: A senior nurse delegates a clinical task to a healthcare support worker.
question: Under the Nursing and Midwifery Council (NMC) Code, what is the registered nurse's responsibility when delegating?
options: Accountability transfers entirely to the support worker once delegated
The nurse remains accountable for the decision to delegate and must ensure the task is within the other person's competence and appropriately supervised
Delegation removes all responsibility from the nurse
The nurse only needs to document that the task was delegated
rationale: The Code requires registrants to only delegate tasks within the other person's competence, ensure supervision and support, and confirm the outcome meets the required standard. The registered nurse remains accountable for the decision to delegate.
source: NMC - The Code

question: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, what must you assume about a person's capacity before any assessment?
options: That they lack capacity until they prove otherwise
That they have capacity unless it is established that they lack it
That capacity depends on their diagnosis alone
That relatives decide whether they have capacity
rationale: The first statutory principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 is the presumption of capacity: a person must be assumed to have capacity unless it is established that they lack it.
source: SCIE - Mental Capacity Act 2005 at a glance

scenario: A patient with capacity refuses recommended treatment, making a decision the team considers unwise.
question: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, does making an unwise decision mean the patient lacks capacity?
options: Yes, an unwise decision proves a lack of capacity
No, a person is not to be treated as unable to make a decision merely because it is unwise
Only if two clinicians agree the decision is unwise
Only if the decision could cause harm
rationale: A core principle of the Mental Capacity Act 2005 is that people have the right to make what others might regard as an unwise or eccentric decision; an unwise decision does not of itself indicate a lack of capacity.
source: SCIE - Mental Capacity Act 2005 at a glance

question: The Royal College of Nursing (RCN) describes restrictive interventions and least restrictive practice. Which of the following counts as a restrictive intervention?
options: Offering a patient a choice of activities
Manual restraint, seclusion, mechanical restraint and rapid tranquillisation
Writing a care plan with the patient
Providing information leaflets
rationale: Restrictive interventions are those that may infringe a person's human rights and freedom of movement, and include observation, seclusion, manual (physical) restraint, mechanical restraint and rapid tranquillisation. The least restrictive option should always be used, as a last resort after de-escalation.
source: Royal College of Nursing - restrictive interventions

question: How many safeguarding principles are set out in the Care Act 2014?
options: Three
Four
Six
Ten
rationale: The Care Act 2014 sets out six safeguarding principles: Empowerment, Prevention, Proportionality, Protection, Partnership and Accountability.
source: SCIE - six principles of adult safeguarding

question: Which set correctly lists the six safeguarding principles of the Care Act 2014?
options: Empowerment, Prevention, Proportionality, Protection, Partnership, Accountability
Consent, Dignity, Respect, Choice, Safety, Trust
Assess, Plan, Implement, Evaluate, Review, Record
Prevent, Pursue, Protect, Prepare, Partner, Promote
rationale: The six Care Act 2014 principles are Empowerment, Prevention, Proportionality, Protection, Partnership and Accountability.
source: SCIE - six principles of adult safeguarding

scenario: A safeguarding concern is raised for an adult with capacity, and staff are deciding how to proceed.
question: What does 'Making Safeguarding Personal' require staff to do?
options: Make decisions on the adult's behalf to keep them safe
Follow a fixed process regardless of the adult's wishes
Engage the adult in conversations to find person-centred, outcome-focused solutions that reflect their wishes and choices
Automatically remove the adult from the situation
rationale: Making Safeguarding Personal is a person-centred, outcomes-focused approach: adults are seen as experts in their own lives, and staff work with them to enhance involvement, choice and control while improving wellbeing and safety.
source: SCIE - Making Safeguarding Personal

question: Which of the following is recognised as a type of abuse under the Care Act 2014 statutory guidance?
options: Financial or material abuse
Constructive criticism
Health promotion
Care planning
rationale: The Care Act 2014 statutory guidance lists ten categories of abuse including physical, sexual, psychological/emotional, financial and material, organisational, discriminatory, domestic abuse, modern slavery, neglect and self-neglect.
source: GOV.UK - Care and support statutory guidance, Chapter 14

scenario: During a ward conversation, a patient expresses views suggesting they may be being drawn into supporting extremist violence.
question: Under the Prevent duty, what is the appropriate action for NHS staff?
options: Ignore it as it is not a clinical matter
Treat it as a safeguarding concern and refer through the trust's Prevent pathway (which may lead to a Channel referral)
Discharge the patient immediately
Report the patient directly to counter-terrorism police without any internal process
rationale: The Prevent duty (Counter-Terrorism and Security Act 2015) requires NHS staff to have due regard to preventing people being drawn into terrorism, recognise signs of radicalisation, and refer concerns as a safeguarding issue via the trust Prevent lead, potentially to the multi-agency Channel programme.
source: GOV.UK - Prevent duty guidance

question: Under Multi-Agency Public Protection Arrangements (MAPPA), which offenders fall into Category 1?
options: Violent offenders sentenced to 12 months or more
Registered sexual offenders subject to notification requirements
Any offender assessed as dangerous
Offenders on community sentences only
rationale: MAPPA Category 1 covers registered sexual offenders subject to notification requirements. Category 2 covers violent offenders sentenced to 12 months or more; Category 3 covers other dangerous offenders assessed as posing a risk of serious harm.
source: GOV.UK - Multi-agency public protection arrangements (MAPPA)

question: The National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) is based on measuring how many physiological parameters?
options: Three
Five
Six
Seven
rationale: NEWS2 uses seven parameters: respiration rate, oxygen saturation, use of supplemental oxygen, temperature, systolic blood pressure, heart rate, and level of consciousness (ACVPU, which includes new confusion).
source: Royal College of Physicians - NEWS2

question: In the National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2), what does a single individual parameter scoring 3 (a 'red score') indicate?
options: No action is needed if the total is low
It triggers urgent review by a clinician competent in acute care, even if the aggregate score is low
It can be ignored until the next routine observation round
It only matters if two parameters score 3
rationale: A single (red) parameter scoring 3 warrants urgent clinical review regardless of the aggregate score, because extreme derangement in one system can signal serious deterioration.
source: Royal College of Physicians - NEWS2 thresholds and triggers

scenario: A patient's National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2) aggregate total is 7.
question: What level of clinical response does a NEWS2 aggregate score of 7 or more require?
options: Routine 12-hourly observations only
Minimum hourly observations and review by a ward-based nurse
Emergency assessment by a clinical team with critical care competencies and continuous monitoring
No change to the current plan
rationale: An aggregate NEWS2 of 7 or more is the high-risk band, requiring emergency assessment by a team with critical care competencies, usually continuous monitoring, and consideration of transfer to a higher level of care. (Score 5-6 is medium risk / hourly; 0-4 is low risk.)
source: Royal College of Physicians - NEWS2 thresholds and triggers

question: The 'Sepsis Six' care bundle from the UK Sepsis Trust should ideally be delivered within what timeframe of recognising sepsis?
options: One hour
Six hours
Twelve hours
Twenty-four hours
rationale: The Sepsis Six is a bundle of six interventions intended to be delivered within one hour of recognising sepsis by frontline staff.
source: UK Sepsis Trust - Sepsis Six

question: Which of the following correctly lists components of the 'Sepsis Six' bundle?
options: Give oxygen, take blood cultures, give intravenous antibiotics, give intravenous fluids, check lactate, monitor urine output
Give aspirin, take an ECG, give oxygen, elevate legs, check glucose, monitor temperature
Give antibiotics only and reassess in six hours
Take observations, document, escalate, wait, review, discharge
rationale: The Sepsis Six comprises: give high-flow oxygen, take blood cultures, give intravenous antibiotics, give intravenous fluids, check serial lactate, and monitor hourly urine output (three 'take' and three 'give' actions).
source: UK Sepsis Trust - Sepsis Six

scenario: You find an adult who is unresponsive and not breathing normally.
question: According to Resuscitation Council UK adult basic life support, what is the ratio of chest compressions to rescue breaths?
options: 15 compressions to 2 breaths
30 compressions to 2 breaths
5 compressions to 1 breath
10 compressions to 2 breaths
rationale: Resuscitation Council UK adult basic life support recommends alternating 30 chest compressions with 2 rescue breaths.
source: Resuscitation Council UK - Adult basic life support

question: According to Resuscitation Council UK adult basic life support, what is the recommended depth and rate of chest compressions?
options: At least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, at a rate of 100-120 per minute
At least 3 cm, at a rate of 60-80 per minute
At least 8 cm, at a rate of 140 per minute
Depth does not matter provided compressions are fast
rationale: Compressions should be to a depth of at least 5 cm but not more than 6 cm, on the lower half of the sternum, at a rate of 100-120 per minute with minimal interruptions.
source: Resuscitation Council UK - Adult basic life support

scenario: A patient is choking, appears distressed, cannot speak, and has an ineffective cough (severe airway obstruction) but is still conscious.
question: According to Resuscitation Council UK, what is the correct sequence of treatment?
options: Give a blind finger sweep, then lie the patient down
Give up to 5 back blows, then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, alternating until relieved
Immediately start chest compressions
Give water to help dislodge the object
rationale: For a conscious adult with severe choking, give up to 5 back blows then up to 5 abdominal thrusts, alternating until the obstruction clears or the person becomes unresponsive (then start CPR). Blind finger sweeps must not be used.
source: Resuscitation Council UK - Adult choking algorithm

question: According to National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidance, when should a patient be risk assessed for venous thromboembolism (VTE)?
options: Only if they report leg pain
On admission to hospital, and reassessed within 24 hours and when the clinical situation changes
Only before discharge
Only for surgical patients
rationale: NICE recommends all patients are assessed for VTE risk on admission, and reassessed within 24 hours of admission and whenever the clinical situation changes, so that thromboprophylaxis can be given where appropriate.
source: NICE NG89 - VTE risk assessment
